details:
**Ethics**
Spinoza's magnum opus, published posthumously in 1677 under the full title Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order. It sets out a complete metaphysical and ethical system in five parts and is the most common giveaway for Spinoza.

**"Demonstrated in geometrical order"**
The method of the Ethics, modeled on Euclid's Elements. Each part begins with definitions and axioms and proceeds through numbered propositions with formal proofs. Its layout later inspired the numbered propositions of Wittgenstein's Tractatus.

**God or Nature (Deus sive Natura)**
Spinoza's identification of God with Nature, the core of his pantheism (or, as some scholars argue, panentheism). God is not a personal creator outside the world but the one infinite substance of which everything is a part, a view that led many contemporaries to regard him as an atheist.

**Tractatus Theologico-Politicus (Theological-Political Treatise)**
Spinoza's anonymously published 1670 work of biblical criticism and political philosophy, called "a book forged in hell" by critics (the title of Steven Nadler's study of it). It argues that Moses did not write all of the Torah, which Ezra may have compiled, that the Torah was the political constitution of ancient Israel and lost its force when that state ended, that miracles reflect the ignorance of the masses, and that prophets were imaginative rather than especially intelligent. It defends freedom of thought, secular government, and democracy, and argues that the sovereign holds authority over public religion. Wittgenstein's Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus echoes its title.

**Cherem (herem) and excommunication**
In 1656 the Talmud Torah congregation of Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community issued a cherem, or writ of expulsion, against the young Spinoza for his heretical views. He spent the rest of his life outside any religious community.

**Substance, attributes, and modes**
The basic structure of Spinoza's metaphysics, set out in Part I of the Ethics, "Of God." There is only one substance, God, which has infinitely many attributes, of which humans know two: thought and extension. Individual things are modes, or modifications, that exist "in" God. The Part opens with a proposition stating that a substance is prior in nature to its affections.

**Rejection of Cartesian dualism**
Unlike Descartes, who held that mind and body are two distinct substances, Spinoza argued that thought and extension are two attributes of one and the same substance, so that mind and body are a single thing viewed in two ways.

**Conatus**
Spinoza's term for the striving by which each thing endeavors to persist in its own being. In the Ethics, a thing's conatus is its very essence, and it underlies his theory of desire.

**"Of Human Bondage"**
The title of Part IV of the Ethics, describing how people are enslaved to their passions, or passive emotions. Part V, "Of Human Freedom," explains how reason and understanding can free a person from that bondage.

**Affects (emotions)**
Spinoza's theory of the emotions, which he treats as natural phenomena following fixed laws. He derives the affects from three primary ones (desire, joy, and sadness) and defines them as modifications by which the body's power of acting is increased or diminished. He distinguishes active emotions, which come from adequate ideas, from passive ones, and his definition later influenced modern affect theory.

**Three kinds of knowledge**
Spinoza's ranking of knowledge into opinion or imagination, reason, and intuitive knowledge. Inadequate ideas arise from the body's confused perceptions, while the highest knowledge sees things "under the aspect of eternity" (sub specie aeternitatis) and produces the intellectual love of God.

**Treatise on the Improvement of the Understanding (Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect)**
An unfinished early work on method that opens with Spinoza deciding whether to change his usual way of life. He rejects the ordinary goods of riches, fame, and sensual pleasure in favor of loving something eternal and infinite, and analyzes false, fictitious, and doubtful ideas.

**Gilles Deleuze**
The French philosopher who wrote Expressionism in Philosophy: Spinoza and Spinoza: Practical Philosophy. He called Spinoza the "prince of philosophers," and in a later work with Félix Guattari he was called the "Christ of philosophers."

**Lens grinder**
Spinoza earned part of his living by grinding optical lenses, a profession often mentioned in clues about his quiet, modest life in the Dutch Republic.

**Principles of Cartesian Philosophy**
Spinoza's 1663 geometrical exposition of Descartes's philosophy, the only work published under his own name during his lifetime. Other minor works include the Short Treatise on God, Man, and His Well-Being and a treatise on the rainbow.
